builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Bad Genius: Counterfactual-Guided Harness Evolution Beyond Task-Specific Shortcuts
summary: CHASE replaces naive task-holdout validation of harness optimization (prompt, memory, retrieval, tool, and control-code edits) with an adversarial Challenger that generates validity-preserving benchmark counterfactuals to neutralize benchmark-wide shortcuts. It costs an additional adversarial search loop, a validity firewall, and a confirmation-set archive on top of each Proposer update, increasing evaluation compute and engineering complexity per harness iteration. It can fail if the Challenger's counterfactual space misses the operative shortcut, if the validity firewall wrongly rejects or accepts transformations, or if the finite archive's statistical guarantees do not transfer to a production benchmark with limited samples.
rationale: The method addresses a real failure mode of automated harness tuning on a single benchmark, but its guarantees and reported gains are demonstrated only on a synthetic benchmark and one real dataset, so a constrained team should pilot it on their own evaluation harness before committing.
technique: Counterfactual-guided harness evolution for robust agent evaluation

claims.statement: CHASE replaces naive task-holdout validation of harness optimization (prompt, memory, retrieval, tool, and control-code edits) with an adversarial Challenger that generates validity-preserving benchmark counterfactuals to neutralize benchmark-wide shortcuts. It costs an additional adversarial search loop, a validity firewall, and a confirmation-set archive on top of each Proposer update, increasing evaluation compute and engineering complexity per harness iteration. It can fail if the Challenger's counterfactual space misses the operative shortcut, if the validity firewall wrongly rejects or accepts transformations, or if the finite archive's statistical guarantees do not transfer to a production benchmark with limited samples.

The abstract reports qualitatively that CHASE 'retains strong released-benchmark gains while substantially reducing gain destruction under valid protocol changes' on a synthetic benchmark and OfficeQA; no multiplicative factor is stated in the abstract.
